newsitem.title: USA: Energy prices sag on Iraq, warm U.S. temperatures.
newsitem.headline: Energy prices sag on Iraq, warm U.S. temperatures.

text.p: Oil prices fell Monday after the United Nations finally cleared Iraq to begin limited sales of crude oil for the first time since the start of the Gulf War.

Forecasts for warm weather in the central United States also hurt prices, temporarily easing worries about tight inventories of natural gas and heating oil heading into the strong winter demand season.

The market's reaction to U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali's clearance of Iraqi oil sales under an oil-for-food accord was muted because approval had been rumoured last week. The deal, renewable after six months, will add almost 600,000 barrels a day of crude to the world market.

Under the pact, the United Nations will ease trade sanctions against Iraq and will allow it to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months. Proceeds must be spent on food, medicine and humanitarian aid.
"Iraq was clearly a factor, but it was no shock that this happened," said A.G. Edwards analyst Bill O'Grady.
"(The Iraqi sale) doesn't change the low (oil) stock situation and the fairly strong demand picture across the world," Sweeney Oil trader Jim Ritterbusch said.
Crude for January delivery lost 32 cents to $25.30 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange, up from a session low of $25.
The temperature forecast weighed more on heating oil, analysts said, noting that temperatures this week in the Midwest could reach the 50s and spread eastward.
"Heating oil is what really took a whipping since it's going to be warmer," said O'Grady.

January heating oil sank 2.53 cents to 72.13 cents a gallon and January natural gas lost 26.5 cents to $3.222 for 1,000 cubic feet. January unleaded gasoline dropped 0.92 cent to 68.88 cents a gallon.

Iraqi oil is returning to world markets for the first time since 1990 when U.N. sanctions were imposed after Baghdad invaded Kuwait. Reports that Boutros-Ghali would approve the on-and-off deal surfaced in the market last week.

Traders noted Iraq will have to build up to its daily exports after being away from the market so long. "It's not all going to happen at once. It will take a while for the oil to reach the market at that capacity," one trader said.
"In the second quarter, Iraq (oil) may make a difference," said another trader, referring to the strong pre-winter demand likely to soak up new supplies.
Soybean prices fell sharply on a slowdown in U.S. exports and beneficial rains in South America's soybean fields.
Brazil and Argentina have enjoyed near-ideal crop weather and additional rains raised prospects for record harvests.
Traders also expressed disappointment with weekly U.S. export figures for soybeans, which were about one-third below expectations at 20.5 million bushels.
January soybeans fell 7.25 cents to $6.88-3/4 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade.

Egypt's purchases of wheat from Argentina and Australia, and not the United States, reminded traders of lethargic U.S. wheat sales and weighed on prices. Weekly wheat exports were below expectations at 12.5 million bushels.

Corn exports for the week were above expectations at 49.6 million bushels, but a private estimate of the size of the U.S. corn crop was above the government's last prediction of 9.27 billion bushels and pressured prices.
December wheat fell 1 cent to $3.90 a bushel and December corn lost 1/2 cent to $2.66-3/4 a bushel.
